questions.question: The most common benign prostatic condition in men over 50 is:

options.explanation: BPH affects the transition zone and causes urinary obstruction.
Prostatitis can occur at any age, but BPH is the most common benign condition in older men.
Adenocarcinoma is a malignant condition, not benign.
PIN is a premalignant lesion, not a benign condition.
Infarction is uncommon and usually secondary to BPH or other conditions.

explanation.overview: BPH affects the transition zone and causes urinary obstruction.
explanation.highYield: Most common benign prostatic condition in men >50 = BPH.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Symptoms include hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia; treatment ranges from medical therapy to surgery.

questions.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia arises predominantly in which zone of the prostate?

options.explanation: BPH nodules originate in the transition zone (periurethral area).
The peripheral zone is the most common site for prostate cancer, not BPH.
The central zone is less commonly involved in BPH.
This zone is mainly stromal and does not give rise to BPH nodules.
BPH has a strong predilection for the transition zone.

explanation.overview: BPH nodules originate in the transition zone (periurethral area).
explanation.highYield: BPH arises in the transition zone.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Enlargement of the transition zone compresses the urethra, causing obstructive symptoms.

questions.question: The most common site for prostatic adenocarcinoma is:

options.explanation: About 70-80% of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, palpable on digital rectal exam.
The transition zone is the site of BPH, not the main site for cancer.
Cancer in the central zone is less common.
This zone is mostly stromal and rarely the site of adenocarcinoma.
Prostate cancer is not diffuse; it has a zonal predilection.

explanation.overview: About 70-80% of prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, palpable on digital rectal exam.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Digital rectal examination (DRE) can detect posterior peripheral zone tumors.

questions.question: The most common histologic type of prostatic carcinoma is:

options.explanation: Acinar adenocarcinoma accounts for >95% of prostate cancers.
Ductal adenocarcinoma is a rare variant with different morphology.
Small cell carcinoma of the prostate is rare and aggressive.
Squamous cell carcinoma is very rare in the prostate.
Transitional cell carcinoma arises from the urothelium of the prostatic urethra.

explanation.overview: Acinar adenocarcinoma accounts for >95% of prostate cancers.
explanation.highYield: Most common histologic type = acinar adenocarcinoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diagnosis is based on glandular architecture and immunohistochemistry.

questions.question: The Gleason grading system for prostate cancer is based on:

options.explanation: Gleason score is the sum of the two most common architectural patterns (primary + secondary grade).
Nuclear atypia is not part of the Gleason system; it is used in other grading systems.
Mitotic rate is not a component of the Gleason score.
Necrosis is not part of the Gleason grading.
Invasion is not part of the Gleason score; it is assessed separately.

explanation.overview: Gleason score is the sum of the two most common architectural patterns (primary + secondary grade).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gleason score is a major prognostic factor for prostate cancer.

questions.question: Prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PIN) is considered a precursor to:

options.explanation: High-grade PIN shows cytologic atypia but intact basement membrane.
BPH is a benign hyperplastic process, not related to PIN.
Prostatitis is inflammatory, not a precursor to cancer.
Infarction is a vascular event, not a precursor.
Sarcomas are rare and unrelated to PIN.

explanation.overview: High-grade PIN shows cytologic atypia but intact basement membrane.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Finding high-grade PIN on biopsy warrants close surveillance.

questions.question: The image shows a cross-section of prostate with nodular enlargement. This is characteristic of:

options.explanation: BPH shows well-circumscribed nodules, often with a whorled appearance.
Adenocarcinoma is usually infiltrative and firm, not nodular and well-circumscribed.
Prostatitis shows inflammation, not nodular hyperplasia.
Infarction shows necrotic areas, not well-defined nodules.
Granulomatous prostatitis shows granulomas, not BPH nodules.

explanation.overview: BPH shows well-circumscribed nodules, often with a whorled appearance.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gross appearance helps distinguish BPH from cancer on pathologic examination.

questions.question: The most sensitive and specific immunohistochemical marker for prostatic adenocarcinoma is:

options.explanation: PSA is a serum marker, not an IHC marker for tissue diagnosis.
PSAP is sensitive but not specific.
NKX3.1 is a prostate-specific marker but less commonly used.
AMACR is overexpressed in cancer; basal cell markers (34βE12, p63) are negative (loss of basal cells).
34βE12 is a basal cell marker; it is lost in cancer, but AMACR positivity is more sensitive.

explanation.overview: AMACR is overexpressed in cancer; basal cell markers (34βE12, p63) are negative (loss of basal cells).
explanation.highYield: AMACR +, basal cell loss = prostate cancer.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A panel (AMACR +, p63/34βE12 -) is used for diagnosis on needle biopsies.

questions.question: The absence of basal cells (by immunohistochemistry for p63 or CK5/6) is a key feature distinguishing:

options.explanation: Benign glands have a continuous basal cell layer; cancer lacks it.
BPH glands are benign and have basal cells, but the distinction from cancer is similar.
PIN retains a basal cell layer, albeit sometimes fragmented.
Prostatitis is inflammatory; basal cells are preserved in benign glands.
The absence of basal cells specifically distinguishes cancer from benign glands (including PIN, BPH).

explanation.overview: Benign glands have a continuous basal cell layer; cancer lacks it.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Immunostaining for p63 or CK5/6 highlights basal cells; their absence confirms malignancy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a risk factor for prostate cancer?

options.explanation: Age is a major risk factor.
African American men have a higher incidence and mortality.
Family history (especially first-degree relative) increases risk.
Age, race, and genetics are major risk factors.
All are established risk factors.

explanation.overview: Age, race, and genetics are major risk factors.
explanation.highYield: Prostate cancer risk = age, African ancestry, family history.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Screening (PSA, DRE) is recommended in at-risk populations.

questions.question: The most common site of metastasis from prostate cancer is:

options.explanation: Prostate cancer typically metastasizes to axial skeleton (lumbar spine, pelvis).
Lung metastases can occur but are less common than bone.
Liver metastases are less common.
Brain metastases are rare.
Adrenal metastases are less common.

explanation.overview: Prostate cancer typically metastasizes to axial skeleton (lumbar spine, pelvis).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bone pain and pathologic fractures may be presenting symptoms.

questions.question: The image shows a bone metastasis with dense sclerotic bone. This is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Prostatic carcinoma produces osteoblastic metastases (increased bone density).
Lung cancer typically causes lytic or mixed metastases.
Breast cancer can be lytic, blastic, or mixed.
RCC causes lytic, expansile metastases.
Thyroid cancer usually causes lytic metastases.

explanation.overview: Prostatic carcinoma produces osteoblastic metastases (increased bone density).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Radiographically, sclerotic lesions in the spine or pelvis in an older man should raise suspicion for prostate cancer.

questions.question: The most common type of testicular tumor is:

options.explanation: Germ cell tumors account for 90-95% of testicular cancers.
Sex cord-stromal tumors (Leydig, Sertoli) are rare.
Lymphoma is the most common testicular tumor in men over 60, but overall less common than germ cell tumors.
Metastatic tumors are less common than primary germ cell tumors.
Sarcomas of the testis are very rare.

explanation.overview: Germ cell tumors account for 90-95% of testicular cancers.
explanation.highYield: Most common testicular tumor = germ cell tumor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Testicular germ cell tumors are highly curable with modern therapy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a risk factor for testicular germ cell tumors?

options.explanation: Cryptorchidism is the strongest risk factor.
Klinefelter syndrome increases the risk of germ cell tumors.
Family history is a risk factor.
Cryptorchidism is the strongest risk factor; also infertility, gonadal dysgenesis.
All are risk factors.

explanation.overview: Cryptorchidism is the strongest risk factor; also infertility, gonadal dysgenesis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Orchiopexy does not eliminate the risk but allows easier examination.

questions.question: The most common testicular germ cell tumor is:

options.explanation: Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumor, usually in young men.
Embryonal carcinoma is less common and more aggressive.
Yolk sac tumor is most common in infants and children.
Teratoma is less common as a pure tumor.
Choriocarcinoma is the rarest and most aggressive.

explanation.overview: Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumor, usually in young men.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Seminoma is highly radiosensitive and has a good prognosis.

questions.question: Seminoma is characterized by:

options.text: Large clear cells with lymphocytic infiltrate and granulomas
options.explanation: Seminoma has sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm, fibrous septa with lymphocytes.
Glandular/papillary structures are seen in embryonal carcinoma.
Schiller-Duval bodies are seen in yolk sac tumor.
Syncytiotrophoblast is seen in choriocarcinoma or in a mixed tumor.
Immature teratomatous elements are seen in teratoma.

explanation.overview: Seminoma has sheets of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm, fibrous septa with lymphocytes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Lymphocytes are a host immune response; their presence is a favorable prognostic sign.

questions.question: The serum marker often elevated in pure seminoma is:

options.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in some cases (syncytiotrophoblast)
options.explanation: hCG can be elevated if syncytiotrophoblast is present.
AFP is not elevated in pure seminoma; if present, it indicates a mixed tumor.
LDH can be elevated as a tumor marker.
Seminoma may produce hCG if syncytiotrophoblast is present, and LDH is often elevated, but AFP is not (if AFP elevated, mixed tumor).
AFP is not elevated in pure seminoma.

explanation.overview: Seminoma may produce hCG if syncytiotrophoblast is present, and LDH is often elevated, but AFP is not (if AFP elevated, mixed tumor).
explanation.highYield: Pure seminoma = elevated LDH (± hCG), normal AFP.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Serum markers are crucial for diagnosis and monitoring.

questions.question: Embryonal carcinoma is a highly malignant germ cell tumor with histology showing:

options.text: Anaplastic cells with glandular, papillary, or solid patterns, often with necrosis
options.explanation: Embryonal carcinoma is aggressive, often with hemorrhage and necrosis.
Clear cells with lymphocytes are typical of seminoma.
Schiller-Duval bodies are seen in yolk sac tumor.
Mature tissues are seen in mature teratoma.
Syncytiotrophoblast is seen in choriocarcinoma.

explanation.overview: Embryonal carcinoma is aggressive, often with hemorrhage and necrosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Embryonal carcinoma is a component of many mixed germ cell tumors.

questions.question: Yolk sac tumor (endodermal sinus tumor) is characterized by:

options.text: Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures) and elevated AFP
options.explanation: Yolk sac tumor secretes AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies.
Syncytiotrophoblast is seen in choriocarcinoma.
Teratomatous elements are seen in teratoma.
Lymphocytes are typical of seminoma.
Psammoma bodies are seen in some carcinomas (e.g., ovarian, thyroid).

explanation.overview: Yolk sac tumor secretes AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Yolk sac tumor is the most common testicular tumor in infants.

questions.question: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant germ cell tumor composed of:

options.explanation: Choriocarcinoma invades vascular spaces and produces hCG.
Monotonous clear cells are seen in seminoma.
Glandular structures are seen in embryonal carcinoma.
Immature cartilage is seen in teratoma.
Spindle cells are seen in sarcoma.

explanation.overview: Choriocarcinoma invades vascular spaces and produces hCG.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Choriocarcinoma is highly aggressive and often presents with hematogenous metastases.

questions.question: Teratoma of the testis contains elements from multiple germ layers. In postpubertal patients, even if mature, it is considered:

options.explanation: Postpubertal teratomas are malignant and can metastasize, unlike prepubertal teratomas.
In children, prepubertal teratomas are benign, but postpubertal are not.
They are already malignant, not precancerous.
They are not indolent; they can metastasize.
Teratomas do not regress.

explanation.overview: Postpubertal teratomas are malignant and can metastasize, unlike prepubertal teratomas.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: All postpubertal testicular teratomas should be treated as malignant.

questions.question: The image shows a testicular tumor with various tissues (cartilage, glands). This is a:

options.explanation: Teratoma contains differentiated elements like cartilage, glands, or neural tissue.
Seminoma is composed of uniform clear cells.
Embryonal carcinoma shows glandular/papillary patterns without mature tissue.
Yolk sac tumor shows Schiller-Duval bodies.
Leydig cell tumor shows Reinke crystals and lipid-rich cells.

explanation.overview: Teratoma contains differentiated elements like cartilage, glands, or neural tissue.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Teratoma may be part of a mixed germ cell tumor.

questions.question: Mixed germ cell tumors are common. The most frequent combination is:

options.explanation: This combination is common, but not the most frequent.
This is less common.
Embryonal carcinoma plus teratoma is a frequent mixed GCT.
This is less common.
This is rare.

explanation.overview: Embryonal carcinoma plus teratoma is a frequent mixed GCT.
explanation.highYield: Most common mixed GCT = embryonal carcinoma + teratoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mixed tumors are treated based on the most aggressive component.

questions.question: Leydig cell tumors are sex cord-stromal tumors that may secrete:

options.explanation: Leydig cell tumors can produce androgens (causing virilization) or estrogens (gynecomastia).
They can produce estrogens as well.
They can produce androgens as well.
Cortisol is produced by adrenal cortex.
Aldosterone is produced by adrenal cortex.

explanation.overview: Leydig cell tumors can produce androgens (causing virilization) or estrogens (gynecomastia).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endocrine symptoms often lead to clinical detection.

questions.question: Reinke crystals are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions characteristic of:

options.explanation: Reinke crystals are pathognomonic for Leydig cell tumor.
Sertoli cell tumors do not have Reinke crystals.
Granulosa cell tumors have Call-Exner bodies.
Seminoma does not have Reinke crystals.
Embryonal carcinoma does not have Reinke crystals.

explanation.overview: Reinke crystals are pathognomonic for Leydig cell tumor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Finding Reinke crystals on biopsy confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question: Sertoli cell tumors are rare and may be associated with:

options.text: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (sex cord tumor with annular tubules)
options.explanation: SCTAT is a distinctive ovarian/testicular tumor linked to Peutz-Jeghers.
Carney complex is associated with cardiac myxomas and pigmented lesions, not Sertoli tumors.
Cryptorchidism is a risk factor for germ cell tumors, not Sertoli cell tumors.
Klinefelter syndrome increases the risk of germ cell tumors, not Sertoli tumors.
Only Peutz-Jeghers is a known association.

explanation.overview: SCTAT is a distinctive ovarian/testicular tumor linked to Peutz-Jeghers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients with Peutz-Jeghers should be screened for sex cord tumors.

questions.question: The most common testicular tumor in men over 60 is:

options.explanation: Primary testicular lymphoma (usually diffuse large B-cell) is the most common testicular malignancy in older men.
Seminoma peaks in younger men (30-40 years).
Embryonal carcinoma occurs in younger men.
Leydig cell tumors are rare at any age.
Spermatocytic tumor occurs in older men but is much less common than lymphoma.

explanation.overview: Primary testicular lymphoma (usually diffuse large B-cell) is the most common testicular malignancy in older men.
explanation.highYield: Most common testicular tumor in older men = lymphoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bilateral involvement and poor prognosis are characteristic.

questions.question: Spermatocytic tumor (formerly spermatocytic seminoma) is a rare germ cell tumor of older men that:

options.text: Has a favorable prognosis and is not associated with germ cell neoplasia in situ
options.explanation: Spermatocytic tumor is indolent, rarely metastasizes, and has distinct histology (three cell types).
It rarely metastasizes.
It is indolent with a good prognosis.
It does not produce AFP.
It does not contain syncytiotrophoblast.

explanation.overview: Spermatocytic tumor is indolent, rarely metastasizes, and has distinct histology (three cell types).
explanation.highYield: Spermatocytic tumor = favorable prognosis, no GCNIS.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Orchiectomy is curative in most cases.

questions.question: Acute epididymitis is most commonly caused by:

options.text: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (in young sexually active men)
options.explanation: In young men, STI pathogens; in older men, coliforms from urinary reflux.

options.text: E. coli (in older men with urinary tract infection)
options.explanation: E. coli is more common in older men, but in young men STIs are the leading cause.
TB is a rare cause of chronic epididymitis.
Viruses (e.g., mumps) can cause orchitis but not typical acute epididymitis.
Fungal epididymitis is extremely rare.

explanation.overview: In young men, STI pathogens; in older men, coliforms from urinary reflux.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sexual history and age guide empirical antibiotic therapy.

questions.question: Fournier gangrene is a life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum, often caused by:

options.explanation: Fournier gangrene is a surgical emergency, often in diabetic or immunocompromised men.
Group A Strep can cause necrotizing fasciitis, but Fournier gangrene is typically polymicrobial.
S. aureus is not the typical cause.
C. perfringens causes gas gangrene, not Fournier gangrene.
Pseudomonas is not the typical cause.

explanation.overview: Fournier gangrene is a surgical emergency, often in diabetic or immunocompromised men.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics are required.

questions.question: The most common type of penile carcinoma is:

options.explanation: Penile SCC is associated with HPV (especially types 16,18) and phimosis.
Basal cell carcinoma is rare on the penis.
Melanoma can occur but is less common.
Adenocarcinoma of the penis is rare.
Sarcoma of the penis is extremely rare.

explanation.overview: Penile SCC is associated with HPV (especially types 16,18) and phimosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Circumcision reduces the risk of penile SCC.

questions.question: Erythroplasia of Queyrat is a form of squamous cell carcinoma in situ on the:

options.explanation: Erythroplasia appears as a red, velvety plaque on the glans.
Shaft involvement is typically Bowen disease.
Scrotal involvement is typically Bowen disease.
Perineal involvement is less common.
Urethral involvement is not Erythroplasia of Queyrat.

explanation.overview: Erythroplasia appears as a red, velvety plaque on the glans.
explanation.highYield: Erythroplasia of Queyrat = SCC in situ of glans.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: It is a premalignant lesion that requires excision.

questions.question: Bowen disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ on the shaft or scrotum. Histologically, it shows:

options.explanation: Bowen disease has disordered maturation and atypical mitoses.
Koilocytes are seen in condyloma, not Bowen disease.
Basal cell hyperplasia is seen in other conditions.
Acanthosis is a nonspecific finding.
Hyperkeratosis alone is not sufficient; atypia is the hallmark.

explanation.overview: Bowen disease has disordered maturation and atypical mitoses.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bowen disease may progress to invasive SCC if untreated.

questions.question: Condyloma acuminatum (genital wart) is caused by HPV types:

options.explanation: Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause benign warts.
HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types associated with cancer.
HPV 31 and 33 are high-risk types.
HPV 5 and 8 are associated with cutaneous warts in epidermodysplasia verruciformis.
Only HPV 6 and 11 are the primary cause of genital warts.

explanation.overview: Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause benign warts.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gardasil vaccine protects against HPV 6, 11, 16, 18.

questions.question: Peyronie disease is characterized by:

options.text: Fibrous plaque of the tunica albuginea causing penile curvature
options.explanation: Peyronie disease results from fibrous tissue formation, often painful erections.
Glans inflammation is balanitis.
Urethral stricture is a different condition.
Priapism is prolonged erection, not Peyronie disease.
Peyronie disease is benign.

explanation.overview: Peyronie disease results from fibrous tissue formation, often painful erections.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment includes medical therapy (collagenase) or surgery.

questions.question: Testicular torsion is a urologic emergency that causes:

options.explanation: Venous obstruction leads to hemorrhagic infarction.
Ischemic necrosis is the outcome.
Coagulative necrosis can occur, but hemorrhagic infarction is the key.
Venous obstruction leads to hemorrhagic infarction.
Torsion causes infarction.

explanation.overview: Venous obstruction leads to hemorrhagic infarction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Torsion requires urgent surgical detorsion (within 6 hours).

questions.question: Hydrocele is a collection of fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis. It is usually:

options.explanation: Hydroceles are common, can be congenital or acquired.
Hydroceles are benign.
Infectious hydroceles are less common.
Traumatic hydroceles can occur but are less common.
Hydroceles can be acquired as well.

explanation.overview: Hydroceles are common, can be congenital or acquired.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Transillumination helps distinguish hydrocele from solid mass.

questions.question: Varicocele is an abnormal dilation of the pampiniform plexus, most common on the left. It can cause:

options.explanation: Varicocele can impair spermatogenesis.
Varicocele is not a cause of cancer.
Varicocele is a separate entity.
Varicocele is not infectious.
Priapism is a different condition.

explanation.overview: Varicocele can impair spermatogenesis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Surgical repair may improve fertility.

questions.question: Granulomatous prostatitis can be caused by:

options.explanation: BCG can cause granulomatous prostatitis.
TB can cause granulomatous prostatitis.
Fungal infections can cause granulomatous prostatitis.
Granulomatous inflammation in prostate may mimic cancer clinically.
All are causes.

explanation.overview: Granulomatous inflammation in prostate may mimic cancer clinically.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Biopsy is needed to distinguish from cancer.

questions.question: Prostatic infarction can occur in BPH and may present with:

options.explanation: Infarcts cause sudden symptoms.
Fever may occur.
Pain can be present.
PSA can spike.
Infarcts cause sudden symptoms and PSA spike.

explanation.overview: Infarcts cause sudden symptoms and PSA spike.
explanation.highYield: Prostatic infarct = acute urinary retention + hematuria + PSA spike.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Infarcts can mimic cancer on imaging and clinical presentation.

questions.question: The most common histologic pattern of prostatic adenocarcinoma on biopsy is:

options.explanation: Most cancers are acinar, with small glands infiltrating between benign glands.
Cribriform pattern is a higher grade.
Single cells are high grade and less common.
Fused glands are Gleason 4 pattern.
Solid sheets are Gleason 5.

explanation.overview: Most cancers are acinar, with small glands infiltrating between benign glands.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gleason 3 is the most common grade; prognosis is good.

questions.question: Perineural invasion in prostate cancer indicates:

options.explanation: Perineural invasion is a route of spread and associated with worse prognosis.
Perineural invasion is a feature of malignancy.
It is not inflammation.
It has prognostic significance.
It does not predict hormone response.

explanation.overview: Perineural invasion is a route of spread and associated with worse prognosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: It is included in the pathology report and may influence treatment decisions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a precursor to prostate cancer?

options.explanation: High-grade PIN is the main precursor; ASAP is a diagnostic category.
Low-grade PIN is not considered a precursor.
ASAP is a diagnostic category, not a precursor.
Only high-grade PIN is considered a precursor.
High-grade PIN is a precursor.

explanation.overview: High-grade PIN is the main precursor; ASAP is a diagnostic category.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: High-grade PIN on biopsy increases the risk of subsequent cancer.

questions.question: The image shows a testis with a well-circumscribed, yellow-brown tumor. This could be a:

options.explanation: Leydig cell tumors are often yellow-brown due to lipid content.
Seminoma is typically creamy white or pale.
Embryonal carcinoma is often hemorrhagic and necrotic.
Yolk sac tumor is usually grey-white and mucoid.
Lymphoma is often a fleshy, tan tumor.

explanation.overview: Leydig cell tumors are often yellow-brown due to lipid content.
explanation.highYield: Yellow-brown testicular tumor = Leydig cell tumor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gross appearance can help suggest the diagnosis.

questions.question: Orchitis can be caused by mumps virus, which typically causes:

options.text: Lymphocytic infiltration and tubular damage, often bilateral
options.explanation: Mumps orchitis in postpubertal males can lead to atrophy and infertility.
Granulomatous inflammation is not typical of mumps.
Suppurative inflammation is seen in bacterial orchitis.
Necrosis can occur but is not the primary finding.
Fibrosis is a late sequel.

explanation.overview: Mumps orchitis in postpubertal males can lead to atrophy and infertility.
explanation.highYield: Mumps orchitis = lymphocytic inflammation + tubular damage.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vaccination against mumps prevents orchitis.

questions.question: Spermatocele is a cystic dilation of the epididymis containing:

options.explanation: Spermatoceles are benign and contain sperm.
Clear fluid is seen in hydrocele.
Blood is not the typical content.
Pus is seen in infections.
Cholesterol crystals are not the typical content.

explanation.overview: Spermatoceles are benign and contain sperm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: They are usually asymptomatic and require no treatment.

questions.question: Adenomatoid tumor is the most common paratesticular neoplasm. It arises from:

options.explanation: Adenomatoid tumor is a benign mesothelial neoplasm of epididymis or tunica.
Germ cells give rise to testicular tumors, not paratesticular.
Sertoli cells are in the testis, not paratesticular.
Leydig cells are in the testis, not paratesticular.
Smooth muscle is not the origin.

explanation.overview: Adenomatoid tumor is a benign mesothelial neoplasm of epididymis or tunica.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: It is a benign lesion that can be confused with malignancy.

questions.question: Malignant mesothelioma of the tunica vaginalis is rare but associated with:

options.explanation: Like pleural mesothelioma, asbestos is a risk factor.
Trauma is not a recognized risk factor.
Infection is not a risk factor.
Radiation is not a known risk factor.
Hormones are not a risk factor.

explanation.overview: Like pleural mesothelioma, asbestos is a risk factor.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A history of asbestos exposure should be sought.

questions.question: Carcinoma of the urethra is most often:

options.explanation: Urethral cancer is often squamous, related to HPV and chronic inflammation.
TCC is more common in the bladder, not the urethra.
Adenocarcinoma is less common.
Melanoma is rare.
Sarcoma is extremely rare.

explanation.overview: Urethral cancer is often squamous, related to HPV and chronic inflammation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: HPV vaccination may reduce the risk.

questions.question: The most common site of metastasis to the testis is from:

options.explanation: Prostate can metastasize to testis.
Lung cancer can metastasize.
Melanoma, prostate, and lung are common primaries; leukemia/lymphoma can also involve testis.
Leukemia/lymphoma can involve testis, but melanoma is a common solid tumor primary.
Colon cancer is less common.

explanation.overview: Melanoma, prostate, and lung are common primaries; leukemia/lymphoma can also involve testis.
explanation.highYield: Most common metastasis to testis = melanoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Metastatic tumors to testis are more common than primary tumors in older men.

questions.question: Bladder outlet obstruction due to BPH can lead to which of the following secondary bladder changes?

options.explanation: Chronic obstruction causes smooth muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and formation of diverticula.
Atrophy is not the initial response; hypertrophy occurs first.
BPH does not directly cause carcinoma.
Papillary necrosis is unrelated to BPH.
Hydroureter can occur with severe obstruction, but the primary bladder changes are hypertrophy and trabeculation.

explanation.overview: Chronic obstruction causes smooth muscle hypertrophy, trabeculation, and formation of diverticula.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: These changes can be seen on cystoscopy and may contribute to urinary symptoms.

questions.question: Acute urinary retention in BPH is a common complication. What is the immediate management?

options.text: Urethral catheterization (Foley) to decompress the bladder
options.explanation: Catheterization relieves obstruction acutely; alpha-blockers and surgery are used for long-term management.
Surgery is planned after stabilization, not emergency.
Observation is not appropriate for acute retention.
Alpha-blockers help but do not relieve acute obstruction immediately.
Suprapubic aspiration is rarely used; urethral catheterization is standard.

explanation.overview: Catheterization relieves obstruction acutely; alpha-blockers and surgery are used for long-term management.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Post-obstructive diuresis should be monitored.

questions.question: Chronic prostatitis can be classified into which of the following categories?

options.text: Chronic bacterial, chronic pelvic pain syndrome (CPPS), and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis
options.explanation: The NIH classification includes categories I (acute), II (chronic bacterial), III (CPPS), and IV (asymptomatic inflammatory).
There are more categories.
This is not the standard classification.
This is incomplete.
This is not the clinical classification.

explanation.overview: The NIH classification includes categories I (acute), II (chronic bacterial), III (CPPS), and IV (asymptomatic inflammatory).
explanation.highYield: Chronic prostatitis = category II (bacterial), III (CPPS), IV (asymptomatic).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment depends on the category; antibiotics for bacterial, multimodal therapy for CPPS.

questions.question: In testicular torsion, the histologic findings after infarction include:

options.text: Hemorrhagic necrosis with congested vessels and interstitial edema
options.explanation: Venous obstruction leads to hemorrhagic infarction, with congestion and necrosis.
Coagulative necrosis is seen in ischemic infarction of solid organs, but torsion causes hemorrhagic infarction.
Granulomas are not a feature.
Lymphocytes are not prominent.
Fibrosis is a late sequel, not the acute finding.

explanation.overview: Venous obstruction leads to hemorrhagic infarction, with congestion and necrosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Early detorsion within 6 hours can salvage the testis.

questions.question: Priapism is defined as a prolonged, painful erection lasting more than 4 hours. It is most commonly associated with:

options.text: Sickle cell disease (vaso-occlusive), leukemia, and drugs (e.g., intracavernosal injections)
options.explanation: Priapism can be ischemic (low-flow) or non-ischemic (high-flow); sickle cell disease is a major cause.
BPH does not cause priapism.
Prostate cancer is not a direct cause.
Torsion is a separate emergency.
Urethritis does not cause priapism.

explanation.overview: Priapism can be ischemic (low-flow) or non-ischemic (high-flow); sickle cell disease is a major cause.
explanation.highYield: Priapism causes: sickle cell, leukemia, intracavernosal injections.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment includes aspiration, intracavernosal injection of sympathomimetics, and treating the underlying cause.

questions.question: Verrucous carcinoma is a variant of penile squamous cell carcinoma characterized by:

options.text: Exophytic, warty growth with minimal atypia and a pushing border, good prognosis
options.explanation: Verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade variant that grows slowly and rarely metastasizes.
Verrucous carcinoma is non-infiltrative and low-grade.
It is squamous, not glandular.
Koilocytes may be present, but the defining feature is the architectural pattern.
Neuroendocrine differentiation is not a feature.

explanation.overview: Verrucous carcinoma is a low-grade variant that grows slowly and rarely metastasizes.
explanation.highYield: Verrucous carcinoma = exophytic, low-grade, good prognosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Complete excision is usually curative.

questions.question: Basaloid carcinoma of the penis is a variant of SCC associated with HPV and characterized by:

options.text: Nests of basaloid cells with high-grade features and an aggressive clinical course
options.explanation: Basaloid carcinoma is a high-grade variant with a worse prognosis.
Warty growth is seen in verrucous or condylomatous variants.
It is squamous, not glandular.
It is aggressive.
Papillary architecture is seen in other variants.

explanation.overview: Basaloid carcinoma is a high-grade variant with a worse prognosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients may require more aggressive therapy.

questions.question: Urethral stricture is a narrowing of the urethra most commonly caused by:

options.explanation: Strictures can be iatrogenic, traumatic, or infectious.
BPH causes prostatic obstruction, not urethral stricture.
Prostate cancer can cause obstruction but not urethral stricture.
Varicocele is a venous issue.
Hydrocele is a fluid collection.

explanation.overview: Strictures can be iatrogenic, traumatic, or infectious.
explanation.highYield: Urethral stricture = trauma (catheterization, pelvic fracture) + infection (STIs).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Treatment options include dilation, urethrotomy, and urethroplasty.

questions.question: Epididymal cysts (spermatoceles) are benign and typically:

options.text: Contain sperm and are palpable as separate from the testis
options.explanation: Spermatoceles are cystic dilations of the epididymis that contain sperm.
Hydroceles transilluminate; spermatoceles may or may not.
They are benign.
They are in the epididymis, not testis.
They do not require urgent surgery unless symptomatic.

explanation.overview: Spermatoceles are cystic dilations of the epididymis that contain sperm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Differentiate from testicular masses by ultrasound.

questions.question: Scrotal ultrasound is useful to differentiate a solid testicular mass from a cystic one. A solid mass in a young man should be assumed to be:

options.text: Malignant (germ cell tumor) until proven otherwise
options.explanation: Testicular cancer is the most common solid mass in young men; urgent evaluation is needed.
Benign tumors are rare.
Infection would show inflammatory changes.
History of trauma would be present.
Torsion would have clinical signs of acute pain.

explanation.overview: Testicular cancer is the most common solid mass in young men; urgent evaluation is needed.
explanation.highYield: Solid testicular mass in young man = cancer until proven otherwise.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Radical orchiectomy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.question: Staging of testicular germ cell tumors includes assessment of:

options.text: Tumor extent, lymph node involvement, and distant metastases (TNM), plus serum markers (S)
options.explanation: Testicular cancer staging uses the TNM system and incorporates serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH).
Gleason grade is for prostate cancer.
Size is part of T, but staging includes N, M, and markers.
Subtype is important, but staging is more comprehensive.
Age is not part of staging.

explanation.overview: Testicular cancer staging uses the TNM system and incorporates serum tumor markers (AFP, hCG, LDH).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Staging guides treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation).

questions.question: In the management of testicular cancer, orchiectomy is performed via:

options.text: Inguinal approach with high ligation of the spermatic cord
options.explanation: Inguinal orchiectomy avoids scrotal contamination and allows high ligation of the cord.
Scrotal approach is contraindicated due to risk of lymphatic spread.
Transabdominal is not the standard.
Laparoscopic is not standard for orchiectomy.
Needle biopsy is avoided due to risk of tumor seeding.

explanation.overview: Inguinal orchiectomy avoids scrotal contamination and allows high ligation of the cord.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Scrotal approach is contraindicated.

questions.question: Germ cell neoplasia in situ (GCNIS) is the precursor lesion for most testicular germ cell tumors. It is associated with:

options.text: Intratubular proliferation of atypical germ cells, often adjacent to invasive tumors
options.explanation: GCNIS is found in seminiferous tubules adjacent to most GCTs.
GCNIS is within the tubules.
It is a malignant precursor.
GCNIS is composed of atypical germ cells, not mature elements.
Inflammation is not the primary feature.

explanation.overview: GCNIS is found in seminiferous tubules adjacent to most GCTs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Detection of GCNIS in a testis with cryptorchidism may prompt surveillance.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of the testicular germ cell tumor staging (S) marker category?

options.explanation: Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH are used to stage and monitor testicular tumors.
PSA is a marker for prostate cancer.
CEA is used for colorectal and other cancers.
CA-125 is used for ovarian cancer.
CA 19-9 is used for pancreatic cancer.

explanation.overview: Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH are used to stage and monitor testicular tumors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Marker elevation can indicate tumor burden and response to therapy.

questions.question: In testicular germ cell tumors, the presence of yolk sac components is associated with:

options.explanation: Yolk sac tumor produces AFP; any yolk sac component elevates AFP.
hCG is produced by syncytiotrophoblast.
LDH is less specific.
AFP is elevated.
CA 19-9 is not a testicular marker.

explanation.overview: Yolk sac tumor produces AFP; any yolk sac component elevates AFP.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: AFP is a sensitive marker for yolk sac elements.

questions.question: The presence of syncytiotrophoblast in a germ cell tumor (e.g., seminoma) results in:

options.explanation: Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG.
AFP is produced by yolk sac.
hCG is the main marker.
hCG is elevated.
PSA is not a germ cell marker.

explanation.overview: Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Even a small amount of syncytiotrophoblast can cause hCG elevation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of classic seminoma on immunohistochemistry?

options.text: C-kit (CD117) positive, OCT4 positive, and placental alkaline phosphatase (PLAP) positive
options.explanation: Classic seminoma expresses c-kit, OCT4, and PLAP; cytokeratin is usually negative.
These are epithelial markers, not typical of seminoma.
Desmin is a muscle marker.
CD30 is positive in embryonal carcinoma.
Seminoma is usually cytokeratin negative.

explanation.overview: Classic seminoma expresses c-kit, OCT4, and PLAP; cytokeratin is usually negative.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: IHC helps distinguish seminoma from other round cell tumors.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about spermatocytic tumor?

options.text: It does not express OCT4 or PLAP, and has a good prognosis
options.explanation: Spermatocytic tumor is distinct from classic seminoma; it lacks OCT4 and PLAP expression and has an indolent course.

options.text: It is highly aggressive and metastasizes early
options.explanation: It is indolent.
It is not associated with GCNIS.
It does not express OCT4.

options.text: It is more common in young men
options.explanation: It occurs in older men.

explanation.overview: Spermatocytic tumor is distinct from classic seminoma; it lacks OCT4 and PLAP expression and has an indolent course.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Orchiectomy is usually sufficient.

questions.question: Radical prostatectomy is a treatment option for localized prostate cancer. The most common side effects include:

options.explanation: Nerve-sparing techniques reduce but do not eliminate these risks.
Hematochezia is not typical.
Bone pain is from metastases, not surgery.
Hematuria may occur postoperatively but is not the main side effect.
Infertility is not a primary concern in the typical age group.

explanation.overview: Nerve-sparing techniques reduce but do not eliminate these risks.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients should be counseled about these side effects before surgery.

questions.question: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer works by:

options.text: Lowering testosterone levels to suppress androgen-dependent tumor growth
options.explanation: ADT reduces testosterone (via LHRH agonists/antagonists or orchiectomy), inhibiting prostate cancer growth.
It decreases testosterone.
Prostate cancer is androgen-dependent, not estrogen-dependent.
COX-2 inhibition is not the mechanism.
ADT is hormonal therapy, not radiation.

explanation.overview: ADT reduces testosterone (via LHRH agonists/antagonists or orchiectomy), inhibiting prostate cancer growth.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Side effects include hot flashes, bone loss, and cardiovascular risk.

questions.question: Which of the following is a rare but aggressive variant of prostate cancer?

options.explanation: Ductal adenocarcinoma is a variant with a worse prognosis than acinar adenocarcinoma.
This is the most common and low-grade type.
Small cell carcinoma is a separate high-grade neuroendocrine tumor.
Squamous is very rare.
Lymphoma is not a variant of prostate cancer.

explanation.overview: Ductal adenocarcinoma is a variant with a worse prognosis than acinar adenocarcinoma.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: It often presents at a higher stage and may require more aggressive treatment.

questions.question: In prostate cancer, the term 'Gleason 4+3' refers to:

options.text: A primary pattern 4 and secondary pattern 3, with a total score of 7
options.explanation: The sum of primary and secondary patterns gives the total Gleason score; 4+3=7 is a higher grade than 3+4.

options.text: A primary pattern 3 and secondary pattern 4
options.explanation: That would be 3+4, which is a lower-grade 7.

options.text: A total score of 7 with no pattern specified
options.explanation: The individual patterns matter for prognosis.

options.text: A score of 7 for the primary pattern
options.explanation: Each pattern is graded 1-5; the score is the sum of two.

options.text: A score of 4 for the secondary pattern only
options.explanation: Both patterns are required.

explanation.overview: The sum of primary and secondary patterns gives the total Gleason score; 4+3=7 is a higher grade than 3+4.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Gleason 4+3 is considered a higher-grade tumor and may require more aggressive treatment.

questions.question: In the TNM staging of prostate cancer, T1c refers to:

options.text: Nonpalpable tumor found on needle biopsy (e.g., due to elevated PSA)
options.explanation: T1c is a clinically inapparent tumor found by needle biopsy.
T2a is palpable in one lobe.
T3 is extraprostatic extension.
T4 is invasion of adjacent organs.
T1a is incidentally found in <5% of TURP; T1c is biopsy-detected.

explanation.overview: T1c is a clinically inapparent tumor found by needle biopsy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Most modern diagnoses are T1c due to PSA screening.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with elevated PSA and a firm, nodular prostate on DRE is found to have a Gleason 8 adenocarcinoma. This is considered:

options.text: High-grade, aggressive disease with a worse prognosis
options.explanation: Gleason 8 (4+4) is high-grade and carries a worse prognosis than lower-grade tumors.
Gleason 8 is high-grade.
Gleason 7 is intermediate; 8 is high.
BPH is benign.
Prostatitis is inflammatory.

explanation.overview: Gleason 8 (4+4) is high-grade and carries a worse prognosis than lower-grade tumors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patients with Gleason 8 often require multi-modal therapy.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-neoplastic condition of the prostate that can mimic cancer clinically and on imaging?

options.explanation: Granulomatous prostatitis can present with a firm nodule and elevated PSA, mimicking cancer.
BPH is a benign hyperplastic condition, but it does not typically mimic a tumor nodule.
Infarct can cause PSA spike but is usually not a diagnostic mimic.
Cysts are usually benign and not difficult to distinguish.
Atrophy is a benign change.

explanation.overview: Granulomatous prostatitis can present with a firm nodule and elevated PSA, mimicking cancer.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Biopsy is needed to distinguish granulomatous prostatitis from adenocarcinoma.
